MS_dataAnalysis

Ben Helms

2026-04-28

Abstract

Measurements of forest structure and surface fuel parameters are a fundamental component of forest inventories in the Southwestern United States. Traditionally, these parameters are estimated using manual field-based methods that are time-consuming and resource-intensive, ultimately limiting sampling intensity and reducing the overall accuracy of inventory campaigns. Recently, active remote sensing approaches have emerged as an alternative to field-based inventory methods. Terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) is one such approach that offers the potential for greater detail and accuracy in inventory data while requiring fewer resources than traditional methods. Previous studies have demonstrated that TLS data can be used to directly measure forest structure parameters and predict surface fuel loads. However, to date, no studies have evaluated the accuracy of TLS approaches in the dry conifer forests of the Colorado Front Range.
In Chapter 1 of this thesis, I investigate the accuracy of single- and multi-scan TLS estimates of mean diameter at breast height (DBH), mean height, canopy base height (CBH), tree density, and basal area measured at 74 Front Range dry conifer-dominated plots. My results show that differences between scanning approaches never exceeded 2.3% for any parameter, suggesting that the more complex multi-scan approach is unnecessary in these forests. Median absolute percent errors from the single-scan approach were smallest for DBH and height (10.7%-12.3%) and largest for CBH, tree density, and basal area (32.3%-38.7%). Bias estimates showed that DBH, tree density, and basal area were systematically overestimated, whereas height and CBH were underestimated. Additionally, errors were greatest in plots that had low tree densities and high understory occlusion from high shrub/regeneration abundance, and low crown base heights. These findings suggest that the single-scan approach can provide an accurate and parsimonious inventory method in forests with high crown base heights and open understories and may enable greater sampling intensities for lower resource inputs than other approaches.
In my second chapter, I investigate the predictive accuracy of single-scan TLS-based models when predicting the fuel loads of five surface fuel components: fine dead surface fuels, large-diameter down dead woody fuels, herbaceous fuels, live woody fuels, and total surface fuels. Three predictive models (random forest, elastic net, and multiple linear regression via leaps and bounds selection) were developed for each component using 166 TLS point cloud-derived predictor variables and a 10-repeat 5-fold cross-validation scheme. My results show that predictions were relatively unbiased; however, normalized root mean square error (NRMSE; 60%-548%) and explanatory power (R2 = -11.16-0.37) varied across modeling approaches, fuel components, and cross‑validation runs. In general, the elastic net model produced the lowest errors, and errors across modeling approaches were smallest and most consistent for fine dead surface fuels, but large and highly variable for large-diameter down dead wood. These findings indicate that TLS-based models can be error-prone and inconsistent when predicting fine-scale fuel loading in Colorado Front Range dry conifer forests and highlight the need for additional research to improve accuracy.
